title: Multi-Region
subtitle: Speed-of-light WAN latency, geographic sharding, and avoiding correlated global outages.
keyTakeaways: Multi-region architectures serve three goals: surviving entire cloud region outages, cutting user round-trip latency globally, and satisfying local data privacy laws (like GDPR).

Speed-of-light in fiber (~200 km/ms) sets a physical constraint: US-East to US-West is ~65-70ms round-trip; transatlantic latency is ~80-100ms. Synchronous writes across regions kill interactive API performance.
Global control-plane dependencies (shared IAM, central databases, global configuration deployments) cause the worst correlated multi-region outages; regions must be engineered as autonomous cells.

sections.heading: WAN Physics and Multi-Region Data Models
sections.body: While Multi-AZ protects against physical data center incidents, an entire cloud region can be disrupted by misconfigured global network routing, regional DNS failures, or severe weather. However, designing across multiple regions immediately runs into the physics of WAN latency.
bullets: The speed-of-light boundary: In optical fiber, light travels at roughly 200 kilometers per millisecond. A round trip between Northern Virginia and Frankfurt takes at least 80 to 90ms under ideal network conditions. Requiring a synchronous two-phase commit across regions for every write will slow user interactions to a crawl.

Asynchronous replication and replication lag: Most multi-region systems write to a local primary database with sub-5ms latency and replicate asynchronously to remote regions. The operational challenge is handling replication lag during failovers, where recently written data may not have arrived in the backup region yet.

Global distributed consensus (Google Spanner, CockroachDB): True multi-region linearizable databases use atomic hardware clocks (TrueTime) or multi-region Paxos groups. They allow globally consistent writes, but each write still pays the mandatory speed-of-light WAN round-trip latency.

sections.heading: Cellular Architecture and Eliminating Correlated Failures
sections.body: Building a multi-region deployment that inadvertently shares a single centralized dependency is worse than running in a single region: it incurs double the operational complexity while remaining vulnerable to a single point of failure.
bullets: Autonomous regional cells: Each region must contain a complete, independent deployment of the application stack, including its own local authentication caches, service discovery, configuration stores, and telemetry pipelines.

Decoupling from cloud control planes: Cloud provider control planes (like IAM updates or container registry APIs) occasionally suffer regional or global outages. A region's data plane must continue serving customer traffic indefinitely even if control plane APIs are completely unreachable.

Phased deployment pipelines: Never deploy software updates to all regions simultaneously. Roll changes out to a canary region, wait several hours to observe error budgets and SLO burn rates, and only then proceed sequentially to other regions.

tradeOffs.pros: Fast local read and write latency (<10ms); isolates outages to a single geographic partition; satisfies data residency regulations.
tradeOffs.cons: Cross-region data aggregation requires batch ETL; traveling users either pay cross-region latency or require shard migration.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Ride-sharing apps (Uber/Lyft), food delivery, regional banking, and multi-tenant SaaS platforms.

tradeOffs.pros: Delivers global serializability and consistency with zero custom conflict resolution logic; RPO = 0.
tradeOffs.cons: Every write incurs 60 to 100ms+ WAN round-trip latency; high infrastructure and cross-region bandwidth costs.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Global financial ledgers, inventory reservation systems, and critical identity/entitlement registries.

interviewTip: Quote realistic latency numbers when discussing multi-region architectures: Intra-AZ is ~0.2ms, Cross-AZ is ~1-2ms, US East-to-West is ~65ms, and US-to-Europe is ~85-100ms. Use these numbers to explain why synchronous multi-region writes cannot meet a 50ms API response target.
